questions.q: In clean architecture, which import breaks the dependency rule?
questions.explain: Dependencies must point inward: adapters → application → domain. The domain importing an adapter points outward, so a change in HTTP formatting could now break the business rules. The composition root is allowed to import everything; that is its job.
options: An HTTP adapter imports the PlaceOrder use case
A use case imports the Order entity
The Order entity imports a function from the HTTP adapter to format its total
The composition root imports the in-memory repository

questions.q: Who owns (declares) the OrderRepository interface, and why?
questions.explain: A port is written from the application's point of view. The adapter imports the port and implements it, so the import points inward even though the call goes outward at runtime. That reversal is dependency inversion. Types are erased at runtime, but the source dependency, which is what the rule is about, is real.
options: The database adapter, because it knows how orders are stored
The application, because the interface describes what the use cases need, and the adapter must implement it
The HTTP adapter, because it receives the orders first
Nobody; interfaces are erased, so ownership does not matter

questions.q: Which of these is a driving (primary) adapter?
questions.explain: A driving adapter starts an action by calling into the application: HTTP handlers, CLIs, scheduled jobs and queue consumers. Repositories, payment gateways and clocks are driven: the application calls them.
options: A background job that calls ExpireUnpaidOrders.execute() every minute

questions.q: Why does Order.place take now: Date as an argument instead of calling new Date() itself?
questions.explain: A function that reads the clock gives different results on each run, so its tests cannot pin the output. The application gets the time from a Clock port, and tests give it a ManualClock, which is how the expiry test moved time forward 35 minutes instantly.
options: Because new Date() is not allowed in TypeScript classes
Because the domain must not allocate objects
Reading the clock is a hidden input; passing the time in keeps the domain deterministic and lets tests control time
Because a Date cannot be stored in a private field

questions.q: What makes Money a value object rather than an entity?
questions.explain: An entity (like an order) keeps its identity while its data changes. A value object is defined by its value and is immutable: plus returns a new Money. The private constructor is how Money guarantees validity, but it is not what makes it a value object.
options: It is stored in the database
It has no identity of its own: two Money values with the same kobo are interchangeable, and it never changes after creation

questions.q: What does the private constructor of Money buy you?
questions.explain: If the only way in is a factory that validates, every instance is valid by construction. kobo is still readable (it is readonly, not private). This is the "make invalid states unrepresentable" idea applied to a class.
options: Every Money in the program went through ofKobo, so no code has to check for fractions or negative amounts again
It hides the kobo field from other code

questions.q: The before-code's order was { status: string } and any code could set status = "paid". What is this called, and what went wrong?
questions.explain: An anemic model holds data and leaves its rules to whoever touches it. The midnight job and payOrder each touched it differently. Putting the state transitions inside Order means every caller gets the same rule.
options: A rich domain model; it had too many rules
An anemic domain model; the rule "only a placed order can be paid" lived outside the object, so a new caller could skip it
A value object; it should have been an entity
A DTO; it should have been validated

questions.q: Why do the use cases return an OrderSummary instead of the Order entity?
questions.explain: The use case is the only path that performs all the steps of an action. Handing out the live entity gives callers a way around it. Plain read-only data can be shown but not acted on.
options: Because entities cannot be serialised to JSON
An adapter holding the entity could call order.cancel() directly, skipping the use case's ownership check, stock release and events
Because TypeScript does not allow classes to cross module boundaries

questions.q: Ada asks to pay ord-3, which exists but belongs to Tunde. findOwn answers order_not_found, not forbidden. Why?
questions.explain: For resources that belong to someone, "not found" for both cases is a common, deliberate choice: a caller cannot probe which ids exist. HTTP does have 403; the choice is about what the answer reveals.
options: Because the repository cannot tell the two cases apart
Answering "forbidden" would confirm that ord-3 exists, which leaks information about other customers' orders
Because HTTP has no status code for forbidden
It is a bug; it should be forbidden

questions.q: Where should "the customer id comes from a verified session token" and "a customer may only pay their own order" live?
questions.explain: Tokens are an HTTP detail, so the adapter authenticates and passes a trusted customerId. The ownership rule must hold for every way in (web, CLI, job), so it lives in the use case, where all of them pass.
options: Verifying the token in the driving adapter (authentication); checking ownership in the use case (authorization)

questions.q: The Catalog port promises that reserve(items) is all or nothing. Why must that promise be part of the port, not left to each caller?
questions.explain: Atomicity depends on the storage: a SQL transaction, a single conditional UPDATE, a lock. The port states the guarantee, every adapter must keep it, and a contract test can check it. Types cannot express it.
options: Only the adapter can make it atomic (for example with one database transaction); a caller reserving line by line could leave some copies held after a later line fails
It does not matter; partial reservations are fine

questions.q: In PlaceOrder, save throws after reserve succeeded. What does the catch block do, and what is it called?
questions.explain: Without one transaction around both steps, the use case undoes the first step by hand. It rethrows because the order really failed. Compensation is imperfect (the release can fail too), which is why a database adapter would rather use a transaction.
options: It retries the save; this is called a circuit breaker
It releases the reserved copies and rethrows; this is a compensating action
It swallows the error so the customer sees success
It publishes an OrderFailed event; this is called an outbox

questions.q: save succeeded, then events.publish throws. Why is "just retry the whole PlaceOrder" a bad fix?
questions.explain: Retrying a whole use case that already has side effects duplicates them. Saving the events in the same transaction as the order, then publishing from that table, makes "saved but not announced" impossible.
options: The order is already saved, so retrying places a second order; the standard fix stores the events with the order and publishes them later (an outbox)
Because the clock will have moved

questions.q: Why does InMemoryOrders store OrderRecords made by toRecord instead of the Order objects themselves?
questions.explain: A fake that stores live objects silently "saves" every mutation. Code that forgets to call save works in tests and loses data in production. The contract test's "changes count only after save" catches this.
options: So a change to a loaded order is invisible until save, as with a real database; otherwise tests pass on the fake and fail in production
Because records are faster to search

questions.q: Where does the persistence mapper (toRecord/fromRecord) belong?
questions.explain: Column names like customer_id and unit_price_kobo are storage details. Putting the mapper in the domain would make the domain depend on the database schema.
options: In the application, next to the ports
In the adapters, because it knows the storage format (column names, ISO strings)

questions.q: A new e-mail adapter wants totals as "₦16,500" (no kobo). Where should that formatting go?
questions.explain: Presentation differs per adapter: JSON, CLI and e-mail all want their own format. Keeping it out of the domain and the application means a new format never touches the rules.

questions.q: The HTTP adapter's status table is typed Record<OrderFailure["code"], number>. What happens when someone adds { code: "book_withdrawn" } to OrderFailure?
questions.explain: A Record over a union of keys requires every key. The compiler turns "forgot to map the new failure" into an error in the one place that must change.
options: The table silently returns undefined for it, and the response has no status
The adapter no longer compiles until book_withdrawn gets a status

questions.q: What is a contract test for a port?
questions.explain: The same tests run against the in-memory and the PGlite repository. If both pass, tests written against the fast fake say something true about the real database.
options: A test that checks the port's TypeScript types compile
One set of behaviour checks that is run against every adapter implementing the port
A test that calls the real payment provider

questions.q: Which import would the lesson's regex-based checker miss?
questions.explain: The pattern looks for import/export … from, side-effect imports and import("…"). require is not matched, and neither is an import built from a variable. Tools that parse the code (dependency-cruiser, eslint-plugin-boundaries) do not have these gaps.

questions.q: For which feature is full clean architecture (entity, use case, ports, mappers) most likely ceremony?
questions.explain: Layers pay off where there are rules to protect and technologies to swap. Opening hours are plain data with no transitions; a simple CRUD handler is clearer there, even inside a clean codebase.
options: Placing and paying orders with stock, payments and expiry
Bank transfers with limits, fees and fraud checks
An admin page that lists and edits the shop's opening hours
Bookings with overlapping-time rules and cancellations

questions.q: A teammate proposes interface Repository<T> { findWhere(filter: Partial<T>): Promise<T[]>; update(id: string, changes: Partial<T>): Promise<void> } for every entity. What is the main problem?
questions.explain: update(id, { status: "paid" }) is the anemic model again, through the repository. Ports should offer only what the use cases need, like save(order) and listPlacedBefore(time).
options: It lets any use case change any field directly, bypassing the entity's rules, and forces every adapter to support arbitrary queries
It cannot be implemented in memory
Nothing; it is the recommended pattern

questions.explain: The map holds the same object that get returned, so the change is "saved" without calling save. A real database would still say placed. That difference is what the contract test catches.
options: It throws, because status is readonly

questions.explain: The second call with the same key returns the first reference and charges nothing. That is why PayOrder sends a stable key: two racing requests for the same order cannot charge twice.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The save fails after the reservation, so the catch gives the copies back, then rethrows, and the caller records the error. Stock ends where it started.

questions.q: Orders were placed at these minutes past 9:00. It is now 9:35 and orders unpaid for more than 30 minutes expire. What does this print?
questions.explain: The cutoff is minute 5. ord-3 was placed exactly at minute 5, and < is strict, so it is not yet due. ord-2 is paid. Boundaries like this are why the expiry test controls the clock.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Each failure's code picks its status from the table. The table has exactly one entry per member of the union, which the compiler enforces.

questions.q: Add a times(quantity) method to Money that returns a new Money, and make ofKobo refuse negative or fractional amounts with a RangeError. The program should print 1350000, then 450000, then RangeError.
questions.explain: times goes through ofKobo, so even a result is validated, and it returns a new value instead of changing price. A value object never changes after it is made.

questions.q: A booking can be "held", "confirmed" or "released". Write the Booking class so that confirm() and release() only work on a held booking and otherwise return "cannot confirm: released" (and so on). The program should print released, cannot confirm: released, released.
questions.explain: With the status private and only readable through a getter, the transitions are the only way to change it, so no caller can confirm a released booking. That is the difference between a rich and an anemic model.

questions.q: The use case below depends on the Clock port. Write a ManualClock that starts at a given date and has advance(minutes), and use it so the program prints false then true.
questions.explain: Because isExpired asks a port for the time, a test can put the clock anywhere. With new Date() inside, this test would have to wait 35 real minutes.

questions.q: Write toRecord(order) and fromRecord(record) for this order. The record uses snake_case and an ISO string for the date. fromRecord must throw an Error for an unknown status. The program should print {"id":"ord-1","customer_id":"ada","status":"placed","placed_at":"2026-09-24T09:00:00.000Z"}, then true, then unknown status "shipped".
questions.explain: Storage is outside the program, so fromRecord checks what it reads, and the type guard lets the compiler accept the narrowed status without a cast. The mapper is the only code that knows both shapes.

questions.q: Write checkImports(files): for each file under src/domain/ or src/application/, report every import whose path contains /adapters/ as "<file> imports an adapter". Use a regular expression over from "…". The program should print the two violations, one per line.
questions.explain: The adapter importing the application is legal, and so is the domain's own import. Run a check like this in CI and the dependency rule stops depending on everyone's memory.
questions.expected:
src/application/pay.ts imports an adapter
src/domain/money.ts imports an adapter

questions.q: Write the CancelBooking use case: load the booking from the repository, answer "not_found" if it is missing or belongs to someone else, call booking.cancel(), save, and return "cancelled" or the domain's refusal. The program should print not_found, cancelled, wrong_status, cancelled.
questions.explain: The use case does the application's steps (load, ownership check, save) and lets the domain function decide the rule. The repository copies on the way in and out, so the save is what makes the change stick.

questions.q: Write hiddenInputs(source) that returns the 1-based line numbers of lines that call Date.now(), new Date() with no arguments, or Math.random(). The program should print [ 2, 4 ].
questions.explain: Line 1 builds a date from a clock port and line 3 from a fixed string, so both are deterministic. Lines 2 and 4 read hidden inputs, which make a use case impossible to test with exact expectations.

questions.q: Write the HTTP adapter's respond(result): a failure becomes { status, body: { error: code } } using the STATUS table, a success becomes status 200 with the total formatted by formatNaira. The program should print 200 {"id":"ord-1","total":"₦16,500.00"}, 409 {"error":"out_of_stock"} and 402 {"error":"payment_declined"}.
questions.explain: Status codes and currency formatting are HTTP and presentation details, so they live in the adapter. The use case only reports what happened; another adapter can phrase the same failures differently.

questions.q: Two stock adapters implement the same port. Write stockContract(name, make), which checks that a reserve that cannot be fully met changes no stock, and prints "<name>: ok" or "<name>: FAIL". Run it on both. The program should print all-or-nothing: ok and line-by-line: FAIL.
questions.explain: The line-by-line adapter took 2 bags of rice before discovering the oil was short, and never gave them back. Both adapters satisfy the TypeScript interface; only a behaviour test run against every implementation catches the broken promise.
